title: The Panhard Dyna Z12’s 851 cc engine: M5, Aérodyne and practical checks
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: Flat-twin design, the change from M5 to M5 Aérodyne, period figures and inspection after storage: the 851 cc engine in its proper Z12 context.
content:
A Dyna Z12 engine appears tiny beside the size of the car. The saloon is 4.58 metres long, seats six and could reach 130 km/h according to Club Panhard data. That apparent mismatch sums up the manufacturer’s method: restrain weight, refine aerodynamics and develop a sophisticated flat twin instead of adding capacity.

Why 851 cc is more informative than “850”

Club Panhard’s technical summary gives a bore of 85 mm and stroke of 75 mm, producing 851 cc. The two cylinders lie opposite one another and the engine sits longitudinally. It has four valves — two per cylinder — operated from a central camshaft. On the M5, valve clearance compensation is hydraulic. There is no water circuit for cooling: air is moved and directed towards the hot parts.

This layout keeps the engine short and its centre of gravity low. It also contributes to a front-wheel-drive arrangement with an almost flat cabin floor. The design creates maintenance practices specific to Panhard. Experience with a conventional water-cooled four-cylinder does not make every setting, assembly procedure or normal sound self-evident.

The M5 fitted to early Z12 cars

The flat twin predates Z12. Engineer Louis Delagarde had developed it continuously since the Dyna X. In 1955, changes to S5 included the distinctive “Eiffel Tower” connecting rods and hydraulic valve-clearance compensation. A few months later the crankshaft was strengthened and a new carburettor adopted; this specification became M5.

Early Z12 saloons built from August 1956 used this engine. The club publishes 42 hp at 5,300 rpm and 6.5 mkg of torque at 3,500 rpm. The manual gearbox has four ratios; developments made in 1956 included fourth-gear synchromesh. These are SAE figures from the period and should not be compared directly with modern output quoted under a different standard.

What M5 Aérodyne changes

For the 1958 model year, Panhard redesigned the movement of cooling air. A turbine replaced the earlier fan and shrouding enclosed the engine to distribute the flow. M5 Aérodyne is the name of this complete arrangement. Claimed power remained 42 hp; the advance concerned cooling and a reduction in noise, especially at higher engine speeds.

The shrouding is therefore not optional decoration. Its panels, joints and air paths belong to the intended operation. A car sold with pieces missing, cut away or poorly secured deserves correction before sustained use. Fresh paint on the covers says nothing about internal condition, but their absence is a visible fault.

A regular Z12 did not leave the factory with a Tigre

M5T Tigre appeared in March 1959, after Z12 production had ended in October 1958. A different camshaft, larger carburettor and enlarged inlet and exhaust passages raised output to 50 hp; the engine was available in later Z16 cars among others. A Z12 may have received a Tigre during its working life, but that conversion does not alter its original specification.

This distinction matters when buying. “850 engine”, “Aérodyne” and “Tigre” are not synonyms. Photographs of the engine, identification plates, carburettor and cooling equipment allow a specialist to narrow down the installation. An invoice for an exchange unit or old rebuild often explains more than fresh paint and a reproduction sticker.

Before waking an engine after long storage

An engine that has stood for years should not perform on demand at the first encounter with a battery and a can of petrol. Old fuel, hoses, oil, turbine condition, freedom of rotation and the presence of all cooling panels come first. Brakes and tyres remain separate from starting ability: an engine that revs does not make the car roadworthy.

Record the recommissioning stage by stage. Pressure obtained, noises cold and warm, leaks, idle stability and response to throttle create a comparison between attempts. A tight spot, metallic sound or large difference between the cylinders is a reason to stop and investigate, not to repeat the same start with more enthusiasm.

Useful observations while it runs

  • Cold start: procedure used, time required and any excessive dependence on throttle.
  • Regularity: contribution of both cylinders, idle stability and response without a marked flat spot.
  • Cooling: turbine, complete shrouding, sound fasteners and unobstructed air paths.
  • Leaks: exact source of oil or fuel traces, observed after cleaning instead of concealed.
  • Ignition and carburation: visible condition, fitted references and available setting invoices.
  • Noises: change with speed and temperature, recorded if specialist advice is needed.

A compression measurement for each cylinder, an ignition check and inspection of the fuel supply complete the first assessment. Values and procedures should come from workshop information for the engine actually installed, not generic guidance intended for another Panhard unit.

On the road, 42 hp does not tell the whole story

The all-steel body brought Z12 weight to about 875 kg, against 710 kg listed for the early Z1. The twin therefore works harder than it did in the all-alloy Dyna Z. It can still move the saloon effectively through the body shape and appropriate gearing, but prefers its useful speed range to being loaded heavily at very low rpm.

A properly adjusted Z12 offers neither modern-saloon silence nor the thrust of a large engine. Its appeal lies in clean response, healthy willingness to rev and agreement between engine, transmission and running gear. If it feels strangled, overheats, vibrates abnormally or falls far short of expected performance, “Panhard character” should not become an excuse that ends diagnosis.

Work that belongs with a specialist

The crankshaft, connecting rods, hydraulic clearance system and several assembly methods belong to a particular engineering culture. For internal rebuilding, tools, clearances and torques from Panhard documentation take priority over intuition. Clubs preserve technical notes, supplies of certain parts and a body of experience that is difficult to replace.

Before purchase, a sensible objective is to identify the engine, assess it without abuse and cost the unknowns. After purchase, a service based on engine number and specification gives a more reliable foundation than changing parts at random as a precaution.
